stem:
A meteorologist looked at the highest wind gust, in knots, recorded each day at an exposed clifftop weather station on the Pembrokeshire coast over 80 consecutive autumn days. She summarised the 80 daily readings in a box plot, which is described here in words.

- Lower quartile $Q_1 = 19$ knots, median $= 24$ knots, upper quartile $Q_3 = 31$ knots.
- The left whisker ends at 12 knots and the right whisker ends at 46 knots.
- Two readings, 53 knots and 64 knots, are drawn as separate crosses to the right of the right whisker.

Each whisker is drawn to the most extreme reading that is not an outlier. Her rule for outliers is that a reading is an outlier if it is greater than $Q_3 + 1.5(Q_3 - Q_1)$ or less than $Q_1 - 1.5(Q_3 - Q_1)$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the interquartile range of the daily maximum gust speeds. (1)
hints: The interquartile range is the length of the box: the upper quartile minus the lower quartile.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the range of the daily maximum gust speeds. (1)

mark_scheme.notes: cao. Do not accept 34 (which uses the whisker end 46).

solution.working: Largest reading $= 64$ (the outlier furthest to the right), smallest reading $= 12$ (end of the left whisker, as there are no low crosses). Range $= 64 - 12 = 52$ knots

hints: The range uses the largest and smallest readings of all, including any readings drawn as crosses.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that the reading of 53 knots is an outlier under the meteorologist's rule. (2)

mark_scheme.for: Compares $53 > 49$ and states that 53 is therefore an outlier
mark_scheme.notes: Needs the correct limit 49 and a conclusion.

solution.working: $53 > 49$, so the reading of 53 knots is an outlier.

hints: Work out $Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ using your answer to part (a).
Finish by comparing 53 with your limit and saying what that means.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Show that none of the 80 days has a gust reading that is a low outlier. (1)

mark_scheme.for: Lower limit $19 - 1.5 \times 12 = 1$ knot, and the smallest reading, 12, is greater than 1, so there are no low outliers
mark_scheme.notes: Needs the correct limit, the comparison with 12 and a conclusion.

solution.working: Lower limit $= Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR} = 19 - 18 = 1$ knot. The smallest reading is $12 > 1$, so no day is a low outlier.

hints: Work out the lower limit from $Q_1$, then compare it with the smallest reading.

parts.label: e
parts.text: A forecaster at a nearby airport uses a stricter version of the rule, with the $1.5$ replaced by $2$. Show that, under this stricter rule, only one of the two readings drawn as crosses would still be an outlier. (1)

mark_scheme.for: Upper limit $31 + 2 \times 12 = 55$, with the conclusion that $53 < 55$ so 53 is not an outlier, but $64 > 55$ so 64 is
mark_scheme.notes: Follow through their IQR from (a), but only if their limit falls between 53 and 64. Both comparisons are needed.

solution.working: New upper limit $= 31 + 2 \times 12 = 55$ knots. $53 < 55$, so 53 is no longer an outlier. $64 > 55$, so 64 is still an outlier. So only one of the two crosses would still be an outlier.

hints: Repeat your method from part (c) with 2 in place of 1.5, then test both 53 and 64.

parts.label: f
parts.text: Assume that the box plot describes the distribution of the daily maximum gust at this station on any autumn day, and that the readings on different days are independent. Six autumn days are chosen at random. Find the probability that on exactly 2 of these 6 days the maximum gust is more than 31 knots. (3)

mark_scheme.for: Uses $p = 0.25$ as the probability that one day's gust is more than 31 knots, because 31 is the upper quartile
mark_scheme.notes: May be implied by $\mathrm{B}(6, 0.25)$ or by $0.25^2$ in an expression.
Must be an individual probability. Using $\mathrm{P}(X \leqslant 2)$ scores M0.

solution.working: 25% of days lie above the upper quartile, so $\mathrm{P}(\text{gust} > 31) = 0.25$. Let $X$ be the number of the 6 days with a gust above 31 knots, so $X \sim \mathrm{B}(6, 0.25)$.

hints: What fraction of days lie above the upper quartile? That gives you the probability for a single day.
Then treat the number of such days among the 6 as a binomial random variable.

pitfalls.text: The IQR is $Q_3 - Q_1$. If you work out $31 - 24$ or $24 - 19$ using the median, you get only half the box and lose the B1.
The right whisker stops at 46, but the largest reading is the cross at 64. If you give $46 - 12 = 34$ as the range, you have left out the outliers and lose the B1.

Many students add $1.5 \times 12$ to the median and get $24 + 18 = 42$, or use $3 \times \text{IQR}$. The limit must be built from the upper quartile: $31 + 18 = 49$. With the wrong limit you lose both B marks.
Don't treat the whisker end, 46, as the outlier limit. The limit is 49, and the whisker stops at 46 only because that is the largest reading below 49.

A common slip is to subtract $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ from the median, giving $24 - 18 = 6$. The lower limit comes from $Q_1$: $19 - 18 = 1$. With the wrong value the B1cso is lost, even though your conclusion happens to be the same.
If you double the whole limit from part (c), or work out $2 \times 31$, you won't get the right limit. Only the multiplier changes: $31 + 2 \times 12 = 55$. Otherwise the B1ft is lost.
31 knots is the upper quartile, not the median, so the probability for one day is $0.25$, not $0.5$. Using $0.5$ gives $0.234$ and loses the first M1 and the A1.
'Exactly 2' needs $\mathrm{P}(X = 2)$. If you use the cumulative value $\mathrm{P}(X \leqslant 2) = 0.831$, you lose the second M1 and the A1.

reasons: 7 word 8-gram(s) also in the Pearson corpus (not whitelisted)

warnings: part d: write B1cso as B1 with 'cso' in its notes
